perspective:
Harold’s available information:

- He knows he is Harold Padilla, a project manager, and that Arthur Begum is a police officer and trusted friend he goes to for advice.
- He feels frustrated and anxious because his project team seems unmotivated and project progress is suffering.
- He meets Arthur at a coffee shop and tells him the team seems unmotivated. He hears Arthur advise understanding each team member’s individual motivation through one-on-one conversations and making people feel valued and understood.
- Harold decides to try Arthur’s advice and feels more hopeful and relieved.
- He tells his team he wants one-on-one chats to understand what motivates them. He hears Team Member 1 say it could be helpful and Team Member 2 say they are open to it. He schedules those meetings.
- After implementing the advice, he observes that the team still is not responding well. He feels disappointed and worried about the project’s future.
- He tells Arthur the team still isn’t responding. He hears Arthur suggest there may be deeper issues such as personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors. Harold decides to investigate further.
- In one-on-one meetings, he hears Team Member 1 report tension between a few team members that is affecting work. He hears Team Member 2 report feeling overwhelmed by the workload and stressed, which makes motivation difficult.
- Harold tells them he will look into resolving conflicts and redistributing tasks to ease pressure, and that their well-being matters to him.
- He then feels optimistic and empowered. He tells the team he will create regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. He hears Team Member 1 and Team Member 2 respond positively, saying it will help and that their concerns are being addressed.
- He only has access to what he personally observed, felt, said, did, and what Arthur and team members explicitly told him.
